thread.title: The Motley Fool's TMFC: Too Pricey And Too Concentrated - The Motley Fool 100 ETF (BATS:TMFC)

author: D.M. Martins Research
title: The Motley Fool's TMFC: Too Pricey And Too Concentrated - The Motley Fool 100 ETF (BATS:TMFC)
text:
Seeking Alpha readers are probably very familiar with The Motley Fool. The 25-year old financial media company provides not only financial news and stock analysis, but it has also been offering investment services that in the case of its flagship Stock Advisor (see image below), the company claims to have produced more than four times the cumulative returns of the S&P 500 ( SPY ) over a multi-year period.
In 2017, The Motley Fool launched its own ETF : Motley Fool 100 ETF ( TMFC ) - although operations did not commence until January 2018. Under my radar until recently, I became very curious to find out whether the fund might be a viable substitute for the more popular index-tracking products offered by the likes of Fidelity or Vanguard.
Credit: Company's website
Let me start with a very high level review of TMFC's key fund characteristics. Motley Fool describes the ETF as follows:
The Motley Fool 100 ETF aims to be a convenient, cost-effective vehicle for individuals who want exposure to stocks recommended by Motley Fool analysts. The Fund is based on an index of the 100 largest domestic companies within The Motley Fool's "recommendation universe."
Right out of the gate, TMFC seems to me like a different breed of ETF. By investing in companies within the manager's recommended list, the fund has an active management component to it. These high-conviction stocks are further defined as being "open buy recommendations in Motley Fool research publications or among the top 150 stocks in The Motley Fool's Fool IQ research database." Who knows, TMFC may even be able to produce the superior returns claimed to have been achieved by the company's stock picking subscription services.
This, in fact, may primarily explain TMFC's sky-high (for an ETF) management fee of 0.50% per year. For comparison, State Street's SPY boasts gross fund expenses of only 0.09%. Over the long run, a $1 million portfolio invested in SPY would save an investor over $1 million in fees alone compared to a similar investment in TMFC, assuming a 30-year time horizon and before-fee annual returns of 8%.
Turning to performance, TMFC has actually done better than the S&P 500 over its very short tenure - at least in absolute terms. As the chart below illustrates, $1,000 invested in TMFC on January 30th, 2018, would have been worth $965. By comparison, the same amount allocated to SPY would have dipped to $920.
But absolute returns do not tell the full story.
First, TMFC behaved more erratically than the broad markets: annualized standard deviation of 21.5% vs. 17.9%. During the fourth quarter correction (i.e., a period when some peace of mind would have been appreciated), TMFC lost an annualized 48.5% against SPY's more moderate 44.1% decline. Motley Fool's ETF also endured more volatility than the S&P 500 during the bear attack. But perhaps even more discouraging, since inception, the daily returns of TMFC and SPY have been highly correlated at a factor of 0.96 - perhaps suggesting that there isn't much uniqueness to the Fool's investment approach compared to what the broad equities market can offer.
Source: DM Martins Research, using data from Yahoo Finance
However, what disappoints me the most in this ETF is the fund's concentration into a handful of popular, high-growth tech names. As the pie chart below depicts, over one-third of TMFC's assets are invested in the well-known FAAMG stocks - Facebook ( FB ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Apple ( AAPL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet's Google ( GOOG ) ( GOOGL ). The allocation is nearly three times as large as that of SPY into these five names.
To be clear, I am and have been at least modestly bullish on these tech companies myself. The problem here is that, when it comes to differentiation, TMFC seems to do a poor job at standing out in the crowd. In addition, I am traditionally very cautious of an overly concentrated investment strategy that puts too much capital at risk from potential deterioration in one narrow sector or group of stocks.
Source: DM Martins Research, using data from Motley Fool's website
The verdict TMFC is perhaps too new of an ETF for me to try and project future results based on the fund's historical performance - its management team still has quite a bit to prove to share owners. It does not hurt, however, that TMFC has in fact beat the broad market on an absolute basis so far and in spite of the 4Q18 broad market correction.
However, I am very much against TMFC's idea of concentrating its capital into only a handful of high-conviction, mega-cap tech stocks. At the very least, if I had been considering investing $100,000 in TMFC and did not mind the portfolio concentration, I would probably choose instead to buy five batches of FAAMG stocks individually and allocate the other $65,000 to SPY at a much lower cost - saving in the process what I calculate to be about $400 in management fees per year.
Therefore, I take a pass on TMFC today, believing that there are cheaper and better diversified ETFs as well as better constructed mutual funds at a comparable price available in the market.
I believe I can produce better risk-adjusted returns than TMFC in the long run.
